# Introduction

`svycoxspline` provides a workflow for fitting and visualizing associations between continuous exposures and survival outcomes using survey-weighted Cox proportional hazards models with natural cubic splines.

The main function, `fit_svycoxspline()`, takes an existing `survey` design object and:

- calculates survey-weighted spline knots and a reference value
- fits a survey-weighted Cox model with spline terms
- generates predicted hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals
- optionally trims the exposure using survey-weighted quantiles
- fits a corresponding linear Cox model
- tests the overall spline association
- tests for evidence of departure from linearity
- tests for linear trend

The basic workflow is:

```text
Create survey design
       ↓
Apply analytic restrictions
       ↓
Fit spline model with fit_svycoxspline()
       ↓
Examine predictions and diagnostics
       ↓
Visualize the association
```

This vignette uses BMI and all-cause mortality in NHANES 2011-2014.

Other complex surveys may use different sampling designs and design variables. Users should construct the survey design object using the appropriate specification for their data before passing it to `fit_svycoxspline()`.

# Load packages

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("MEB-PASS/svycoxspline")
```

```{r}
library(svycoxspline)
library(survey)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Prepare the data

The example data are included with the package.

```{r}
dat <- data.table::fread(
  system.file("data", "nhanes_spline_data.csv", package = "svycoxspline"),
  data.table = FALSE
)
```

The data include the NHANES survey design variables (`sdmvpsu`, `sdmvstra`, and `mec4yr`), BMI, follow-up time, mortality status, age, and sex.

You can inspect the available variables with:

```{r}
names(dat)
head(dat)
```

# Create the survey design

NHANES is a complex survey, so the analysis should use the appropriate primary sampling units, strata, and survey weights.

```{r}
NHANES_all <- svydesign(
  data = dat,
  id = ~sdmvpsu,
  strata = ~sdmvstra,
  weights = ~mec4yr,
  nest = TRUE
)
```

For this example, restrict the analysis to participants aged 40 years or older with BMI between 10 and 60 kg/m$^2$.

```{r}
NHANES_qc <- subset(
  NHANES_all,
  age >= 40 & bmi > 10 & bmi < 60
)
```

**Important:** Create the survey design and assign survey weights before applying analytic or subgroup restrictions. Use `survey::subset()` to restrict the survey design so that the survey design information and weights are retained.

# Fit a spline model

A model uses BMI as the exposure, mortality as the event, and follow-up time in months, adjusting for age and sex.

```{r, message=FALSE, results='hide'}
res_bmi <- fit_svycoxspline(
  design = NHANES_qc,
  exposure_var = "bmi",
  time_var = "fu_months_int",
  event_var = "mortality",
  covariates = c("age", "factor(sex)"),
  trim_probs = c(0.01, 0.99),
  knot_probs = c(0.05, 0.50, 0.95),
  ref_prob = 0.10,
  report_points = c(25, 30),
  grid_by = 1,
  round_to = 1
)
```

The main arguments are:

| Argument | Purpose | Default | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `trim_probs` | Lower and upper survey-weighted quantiles defining the exposure range used for modeling | `c(0.01, 0.99)` | `c(0.01, 0.99)` or `NULL` |
| `knot_probs` | Survey-weighted quantiles used to place spline knots and define the boundary knots | `c(0.05, 0.50, 0.95)` | `c(0.05, 0.50, 0.95)` |
| `ref_prob` | Survey-weighted quantile defining the HR = 1 reference value | `0.10` | `0.10` |
| `report_points` | Exposure values at which HRs and 95% CIs are returned | `NULL` | `c(25, 30)` |
| `grid_by` | Spacing of exposure values used for prediction | `1` | `1` |
| `round_to` | Increment used to round the reference value and prediction limits; `1` rounds to whole units, `0.1` to tenths, and `10` to multiples of 10 | `1` | `1` |

### Choosing the spline settings

`trim_probs` defines the exposure range used for model fitting and prediction. For example, `c(0.01, 0.99)` uses the survey-weighted 1st and 99th percentiles. Set `trim_probs = NULL` to retain the full observed exposure range.

`knot_probs` defines the survey-weighted percentiles used to place spline knots. More probabilities can be supplied when additional knots are appropriate. Sparse exposure distributions can produce unstable or non-unique knots.

`ref_prob` defines the exposure percentile used as the HR = 1 reference. For example, `ref_prob = 0.10` uses the survey-weighted 10th percentile as the reference.

`report_points` specifies exposure values at which HRs and 95% CIs are returned. For example, `report_points = c(25, 30)` returns estimates at BMI values of 25 and 30 kg/m².

`grid_by` controls the spacing of exposure values used for predictions.

`round_to` controls the increment used to round the reference value and the lower and upper limits of the prediction grid. The default is `round_to = 1`, which rounds these values to the nearest whole unit. For exposures where smaller increments are meaningful, users can specify a smaller value. For example, `round_to = 0.1` rounds to the nearest 0.1 units, while `round_to = 10` rounds to the nearest 10 units. Choose a value that is appropriate for the scale and interpretation of the exposure.

# Examine the results

The fitted object contains the model fits, predictions, spline knots, reference value, and association tests.

```{r}
names(res_bmi)
```

The main returned objects are:

| Returned object | Description |
|:---|:---|
| `fit_spline` | Survey-weighted Cox model containing natural spline terms |
| `fit_linear` | Corresponding survey-weighted Cox model with a linear exposure term |
| `fit_nonlinearity` | Equivalent reparameterization of the spline model used for the test of non-linearity |
| `pred_spline` | Predicted HRs and 95% CIs from the spline model |
| `pred_linear` | Predicted HRs and 95% CIs from the linear model |
| `pred_points` | Predicted HRs and 95% CIs at user-specified `report_points` |
| `knots` | Exposure values corresponding to the spline knots |
| `ref_val` | Exposure value used as the HR = 1 reference |
| `overall_p` | Numeric p-value for the overall spline association |
| `overall_p_label` | Formatted p-value for the overall spline association |
| `nonlinearity_p` | Numeric p-value for the Wald test of departure from linearity |
| `nonlinearity_p_label` | Formatted p-value for the test of non-linearity |
| `nonlinear_terms` | Spline terms jointly tested for departure from linearity |
| `trend_p` | Numeric p-value for the linear trend test |
| `trend_p_label` | Formatted p-value for the linear trend test |
| `design_clipped` | Survey design used for model fitting after optional trimming |

The fitted object also contains internal diagnostics used to verify the spline reparameterization:

- `x_reconstruction_error`
- `spline_space_error`
- `reparameterization_lp_difference`

These values should be approximately zero when the reparameterization successfully reproduces the original natural spline model.

Inspect the reference value, knots, association tests, and predictions with:

```{r}
res_bmi$knots
res_bmi$ref_val

res_bmi$overall_p
res_bmi$overall_p_label

res_bmi$nonlinearity_p
res_bmi$nonlinearity_p_label

res_bmi$trend_p
res_bmi$trend_p_label

head(res_bmi$pred_spline)
```

The three association tests answer different questions:

- `overall_p` tests whether the spline terms are jointly associated with the outcome.
- `nonlinearity_p` tests whether the spline association departs from linearity.
- `trend_p` tests the continuous exposure term in the corresponding linear Cox model.

The prediction data contain the exposure value, estimated HR, and lower and upper 95% confidence limits.

Inspect the estimated HRs and 95% CIs at the specified exposure values:

```{r}
res_bmi$pred_points[, c("bmi", "HR", "lo", "hi")]
```

## Interpreting the test for non-linearity

`fit_svycoxspline()` assesses departure from linearity using a Wald test. The fitted natural spline is reparameterized so that the exposure is included explicitly as the linear component, with the remaining spline terms representing departures from linearity. The reparameterization spans the same natural spline space as the model used to estimate the exposure-response curve.

A joint Wald test of the nonlinear terms is then used to test the null hypothesis that the exposure-response association is linear.

A smaller p-value provides evidence that the association departs from a linear relationship. A larger p-value indicates insufficient evidence to reject linearity. The test should be interpreted alongside the estimated curve, confidence intervals, exposure distribution, and model assumptions rather than in isolation.

### Table of results

The predicted hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals at all exposure values along the spline curve can be exported as a results table. The table also includes p-values for the overall spline association, non-linearity, and linear trend.

```{r}
results_table <- res_bmi$pred_spline

results_table$`HR (95% CI)` <- sprintf(
  "%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
  results_table$HR,
  results_table$lo,
  results_table$hi
)

# Add association test p-values
results_table$p_overall <- res_bmi$overall_p
results_table$p_nonlinearity <- res_bmi$nonlinearity_p
results_table$p_trend <- res_bmi$trend_p

# Identify exposure variable
exposure_var <- names(results_table)[1]

# Identify reference value
results_table$reference <- ifelse(
  results_table[[exposure_var]] == res_bmi$ref_val,
  "Reference",
  ""
)

# Keep exposure, formatted HR (95% CI), p-values,
# and reference indicator
results_table <- results_table[
  , c(
    exposure_var,
    "HR (95% CI)",
    "p_overall",
    "p_nonlinearity",
    "p_trend",
    "reference"
  )
]

head(results_table)
```

### Plot the association

The predicted hazard ratios can be visualized directly with `ggplot2`.

```{r}
ggplot(res_bmi$pred_spline, aes(x = bmi, y = HR)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(
    data = res_bmi$pred_points,
    aes(xintercept = bmi),
    linetype = "dotted"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = res_bmi$pred_points,
    aes(x = bmi, y = HR),
    size = 3
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = res_bmi$pred_points,
    aes(
      x = bmi,
      y = HR,
      label = sprintf(
        "BMI = %.0f\n%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
        bmi, HR, lo, hi
      )
    ),
    nudge_y = 0.20,
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "NHANES 2011-2014",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Reference = ",
      res_bmi$ref_val,
      "; Knots = (",
      paste(round(res_bmi$knots, 1), collapse = ", "),
      ")",
      "; p-nonlinear = ",
      res_bmi$nonlinearity_p_label
    ),
    x = "Body mass index (kg/m²)",
    y = "Adjusted hazard ratio (95% CI)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Compare spline and linear associations

`fit_svycoxspline()` also fits a corresponding linear Cox model. The two prediction sets can be combined to compare the fitted associations.

```{r}
pred_compare <- rbind(
  transform(res_bmi$pred_spline, model = "Spline"),
  transform(res_bmi$pred_linear, model = "Linear")
)
```

```{r}
ggplot(pred_compare, aes(x = bmi, y = HR, linetype = model)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = res_bmi$pred_spline,
    aes(x = bmi, ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "NHANES 2011-2014",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Reference = ",
      res_bmi$ref_val,
      "; Knots = (",
      paste(round(res_bmi$knots, 1), collapse = ", "),
      ")",
      "; p-nonlinear = ",
      res_bmi$nonlinearity_p_label
    ),
    x = "Body mass index (kg/m²)",
    y = "Adjusted hazard ratio (95% CI)",
    linetype = "Model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The spline model allows the association to vary across the exposure range, while the linear model assumes a linear association on the log-hazard scale.

# Sex-stratified analyses

The same workflow can be applied separately within subgroups. First create subgroup survey designs from the existing survey design.

```{r}
NHANES_qc_female <- subset(NHANES_qc, sex == "Female")
NHANES_qc_male <- subset(NHANES_qc, sex == "Male")
```

Because each model is fitted within a single sex stratum, sex is not included as a covariate.

```{r}
res_female <- fit_svycoxspline(
  design = NHANES_qc_female,
  exposure_var = "bmi",
  time_var = "fu_months_int",
  event_var = "mortality",
  covariates = "age",
  trim_probs = c(0.01, 0.99),
  knot_probs = c(0.05, 0.50, 0.95),
  ref_prob = 0.10,
  report_points = c(25, 30),
  grid_by = 1,
  round_to = 1
)

res_male <- fit_svycoxspline(
  design = NHANES_qc_male,
  exposure_var = "bmi",
  time_var = "fu_months_int",
  event_var = "mortality",
  covariates = "age",
  trim_probs = c(0.01, 0.99),
  knot_probs = c(0.05, 0.50, 0.95),
  ref_prob = 0.10,
  report_points = c(25, 30),
  grid_by = 1,
  round_to = 1
)
```

Predictions can then be combined for visualization.

```{r}
pred_combined <- rbind(
  transform(res_female$pred_spline, sex = "Female"),
  transform(res_male$pred_spline, sex = "Male")
)

points_combined <- rbind(
  transform(res_female$pred_points, sex = "Female"),
  transform(res_male$pred_points, sex = "Male")
)
```

### Table of results

Estimates can be stored in a table.

```{r}
results_table_sex <- pred_combined

results_table_sex$`HR (95% CI)` <- sprintf(
  "%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
  results_table_sex$HR,
  results_table_sex$lo,
  results_table_sex$hi
)

results_table_sex$wald_p_nonlinearity <- ifelse(
  results_table_sex$sex == "Female",
  res_female$nonlinearity_p,
  res_male$nonlinearity_p
)

# Keep exposure, sex, formatted HR (95% CI), and Wald p-value
exposure_var <- names(results_table_sex)[1]

results_table_sex <- results_table_sex[
  , c(
    exposure_var,
    "sex",
    "HR (95% CI)",
    "wald_p_nonlinearity"
  )
]

# Specify reference row
results_table_sex$reference <- ifelse(
  (results_table_sex$sex == "Female" &
     results_table_sex[[exposure_var]] == res_female$ref_val) |
    (results_table_sex$sex == "Male" &
       results_table_sex[[exposure_var]] == res_male$ref_val),
  "Reference",
  ""
)

head(results_table_sex)
```

### Plot the association

Subgroup predictions can be plotted.

Note that exposure quantiles are calculated separately within each subgroup, so knot locations and reference values may differ between subgroups.

```{r}
ggplot(
  pred_combined,
  aes(
    x = bmi,
    y = HR,
    colour = sex,
    fill = sex,
    linetype = sex
  )
) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
    alpha = 0.2,
    colour = NA
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    data = points_combined,
    aes(xintercept = bmi),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    linetype = "dotted"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = points_combined,
    aes(x = bmi, y = HR, colour = sex),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 3
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = subset(points_combined, sex == "Female"),
    aes(
      x = bmi,
      y = HR,
      colour = sex,
      label = sprintf(
        "BMI = %.0f\n%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
        bmi, HR, lo, hi
      )
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    nudge_y = -0.18,
    size = 2.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = subset(points_combined, sex == "Male"),
    aes(
      x = bmi,
      y = HR,
      colour = sex,
      label = sprintf(
        "BMI = %.0f\n%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
        bmi, HR, lo, hi
      )
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    nudge_y = 0.18,
    size = 2.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "NHANES 2011-2014",
    x = "Body mass index (kg/m²)",
    y = "Adjusted hazard ratio (95% CI)",
    colour = "Sex",
    fill = "Sex",
    linetype = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Important considerations

`fit_svycoxspline()` assumes that the supplied object already represents the survey design and analytic population of interest. Define survey weights, strata, and clusters before calling the function.

Apply analytic and subgroup restrictions using `survey::subset()` after creating the survey design.

Choose exposure trimming, knot locations, and the reference value based on the exposure distribution and scientific question. Sparse data near the exposure extremes can produce unstable estimates and wide confidence intervals.

Interpret the test for non-linearity together with the estimated curve, confidence intervals, exposure distribution, and model assumptions.

Standard Cox proportional hazards diagnostics, including assessment of the proportional hazards assumption, should be performed separately.
